title: Produce and use spreadsheets for business

lessons.title: Spreadsheet basics
lessons.html:
What a spreadsheet does

A spreadsheet program, such as Microsoft Excel, LibreOffice Calc or Google Sheets, arranges data in a grid so you can calculate, sort, analyse and present it. On a farm or in an abattoir it can be used for slaughter tallies, stock registers, payroll hours, feed costs, temperature logs and budgets.

Parts of a spreadsheet

  • Workbook: the file. It can contain several worksheets (tabs).
  • Columns have letters (A, B, C ...) and rows have numbers (1, 2, 3 ...).
  • A cell is where a column and row meet, named by its address, for example B4.
  • A range is a group of cells, for example B2:B10.
  • The formula bar shows the contents of the selected cell.

Entering data well

  • Put headings in the first row, one heading per column, for example Date, Carcass number, Species, Mass (kg).
  • One record per row. Do not leave blank rows inside the data.
  • Keep one kind of data per column. Do not type "kg" in the number cells; put the unit in the heading.
  • Use a consistent date format.

Formatting

  • Number formats: currency (R), decimal places, percentages, dates.
  • Bold headings, adjust column width, wrap text, borders.
  • Freeze the top row so headings stay visible when you scroll.
  • Conditional formatting can highlight values, for example temperatures above a limit in red.

Saving and protecting work

Save often, with a clear file name such as "Slaughter tally 2026-10.xlsx". Keep backups. Protect sheets or files with passwords where data is confidential, such as wages, and follow the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA) when spreadsheets contain personal information.

lessons.title: Formulas and functions
lessons.html:
Making the spreadsheet calculate

Every formula starts with an equals sign (=). Use cell addresses, not typed numbers, so results update automatically when data changes.

Basic operators

OperatorMeaningExample
+Add=B2+C2
-Subtract=B2-C2
*Multiply=B2*C2
/Divide=B2/C2

Common functions

  • =SUM(B2:B20) adds the range.
  • =AVERAGE(B2:B20) gives the mean.
  • =MAX() and =MIN() find the highest and lowest values.
  • =COUNT(B2:B20) counts cells with numbers.
  • =IF(C2>7,"Too warm","OK") tests a condition.
  • =ROUND(B2,1) rounds to one decimal place.

Relative and absolute references

When you copy a formula down a column, cell references change automatically (relative references). Sometimes one reference must stay fixed, such as a price per kilogram in cell F1. Use a dollar sign to make it absolute: =B2*$F$1. Copied down, it becomes =B3*$F$1, =B4*$F$1 and so on.

Example: carcass payment

Column B has carcass mass in kg, cell F1 has the price of R65.00 per kg. In C2 type =B2*$F$1 and copy down. A 240 kg carcass gives R15 600. At the bottom, =SUM(C2:C51) gives the total payment.

Checking formulas

Estimate the answer first. Error messages such as #DIV/0! (dividing by zero) or #VALUE! (text where a number is expected) show something is wrong. Check your ranges include all the rows.

Save a copy before changing formulas, so you can go back if something goes wrong.

Use the Show Formulas option to see all formulas at once when checking a sheet, and test formulas with simple numbers you can calculate by hand.

lessons.title: Analysing and presenting data
lessons.html:
Turning data into information

Sorting and filtering

  • Sort rows by a column, for example from heaviest to lightest carcass, or by date. Select the whole data range first so rows stay together.
  • Filter shows only rows that match a condition, for example only species "Sheep" or only temperatures above the limit.

Summary tables

Functions such as SUMIF and COUNTIF summarise by category: =COUNTIF(C2:C200,"Cattle") counts cattle; =SUMIF(C2:C200,"Cattle",D2:D200) adds their mass. A pivot table creates totals and averages by category without writing formulas.

Charts

Chart typeBest for
Column or barComparing categories, such as slaughter numbers per species
LineTrends over time, such as daily chiller temperatures
PieParts of a whole, used sparingly with few categories

Give every chart a clear title, axis labels with units, and a legend if there is more than one series.

Printing and sharing

  • Use Print Preview. Set orientation (portrait or landscape), fit to page width, and print titles so headings repeat on every page.
  • Add a header or footer with the report name, date and page numbers.
  • Save as PDF to share a report that others should not change.

Using the results in business

A weekly summary of mass, payment and condemnations per supplier helps managers see trends, spot problems and make decisions. Always check the data before presenting it.

Key points

  • Use one record per row, one kind of data per column, and clear headings.
  • Formulas start with = and should use cell addresses.
  • Use $ to make an absolute reference when copying formulas.
  • Sort, filter, SUMIF, COUNTIF and pivot tables summarise data.
  • Choose the right chart, label it clearly and use Print Preview.
